item.title: Everpure's head-turning fiscal 2028 guidance
item.description:
Financial analysts were told Everpure is at an inflexion point with three growth drivers and accelerated growth leading to a stunning fiscal 2028 revenue projection.

CTO Rob Lee said the core all-flash array business, incuding an AI component, is growing steadily. But there are three new growth markets which do not overlap;

  • Modern data software ( Portworx for Kubernetes data management, Pure Protect for

backup and cyber recovery, Everpure Cloud for hybrid- and multi-cloud data mobility, Data Intelligence from 1Touch, and Data Stream), which organizes, governs, and makes data accessible for AI, not just storing it,

  • Scale AI providing GPU-attached storage for exabyte-scale AI workloads at Neoclouds and larger enterprises,

  • Hyperscale solutions licensing DirectFlash Module intellectual property to the largest hyperscalers (with 2 design wins already and limited competitive options).

Everpure reported fiscal 2026 revenues of $3.66 billion, up 16 percent YoY. After reporting a terrific fiscal Q2 fy 2027, it’s guiding fiscal 2027 revenues to be $5.05 billion ± $20 million; up $500 million on its initial fy2027 guidance 3 months prior, and a 38 percent jump on fiscal 2026.

Now it has pushed the forecasting boat out further, telling the analysts it expects fiscal 2028 revenues to be $7.15 billion ± $150 million, representing a 41.6 percent uplift on fiscal 2027. That’s because, it says, its four growth drivers come together ad operate in concert.

An Everpure annual revenue history chart with the estimated fy 2027 and 2028 mid-point numbers shows this accelerated growth clearly;

CEO Charles Giancarlo and CFO Tarek Robbiati have put themselves out in the open for analyst and investor ire if the company fails to meet these targets, and are setting themselves up as heroes if it does reach them.

William Blair analyst Jason Ader said this was “head-turning guidance” with Everpure’s execs providing “a meaningful reset of the company's long-term growth narrative and financial profile.”

He pointed out Everpure execs “highlighted 8 consecutive quarters of accelerating revenue growth and 12 consecutive years of enterprise storage share gains, arguing that the current acceleration reflects structural improvements in the business rather than cyclical tailwinds.”

Everpure “management believes Everpure’s future growth profile will increasingly be driven by multiple independent growth vectors, not enterprise storage share gains alone. Notably, management repeatedly characterized the company's current position as an “inflection point,” emphasizing that the acceleration is “durable” and “not a spike.”

He reckons the three new growth vectors (markets) roughly double Everpure’s TAM and together are expected to reach 20 percent of total revenue by fiscal 2030.

item.title: Xinnor simplifies and extends RAID-based fast NAS management
item.description:
Xinnor adds comprehensive RAID, filesystems, NFS and networking control plane and previews its extension via MCP to AI assistants and separately to parallel NFS Lattice co-ordination.

Xinnor found that its RAID SW could be parlayed into a fast network-attached file system (NAS) and its xiNAS product was introduced earlier this year as a high-performance NFS over RDMA storage system. It came on Supermicro storage servers with AMD EPYC processors and PCIe Gen5 NVMe drives. V3.13 xiNAS is the latest production version of this with unified management, automation and diagnostics.

xiNAS 3.13 introduces a single control plane for storage provisioning, NFS configuration, health inspection and configuration history. Whether an operation comes from the terminal interface, CLI, REST API or MCP-client, xiNAS follows the same workflow: it builds a end-to-end plan for a particular task showing what will change, checks permissions, applies the approved operation and records it in the audit log.

Operations that can alter or destroy data require the appropriate role and explicit confirmation. This gives administrators a consistent way to manage RAID, filesystems, NFS and networking instead of working through separate management paths.

An xiNAS 3.14 technology preview extends this control plane to MCP -compatible AI assistants and automation tools. Administrators can use an AI client to inspect system health, investigate unavailable shares, review changes or prepare configuration operations.

Sergei Platonov, VP of Strategy at Xinnor, said: “AI can make storage administration much easier, but it should not bypass the controls that make infrastructure predictable and safe. In the 3.14 preview, an assistant can inspect the system, explain what it finds and prepare an operation, while permissions, the execution plan and final confirmation remain under xiNAS control.”

The AI client does not receive shell access. Requests are mapped to defined xiNAS operations and remain subject to the same permissions, planning, confirmation and auditing rules used by other management interfaces. Diagnostic results also record which checks succeeded, failed, timed out or could not be performed, so missing information is not treated as evidence of a healthy system.

An xiNAS 3.15 technology preview explores a separate problem in scale-out pNFS environments: how a coordination layer could take the actual condition of storage servers into account when placing new data.

In the v3.15 preview, xiNAS publishes the condition of the RAID, filesystem and NFS layers behind each share. A connector can make this information available to pNFS Lattice, an open-source metadata and coordination layer for pNFS. This creates a basis for evaluating placement policies that could avoid servers that are rebuilding, degraded or unavailable.

xiNAS 3.13 is available now as the current stable release. Source branches for xiNAS 3.14 and 3.15 are available separately for technical evaluation. The 3.15 work is an early technology preview intended for tech inspection and development.

Sergei Platonov will discuss the architecture and safety model behind the MCP preview at the SNIA Developer Conference 2026 on September 30.

item.title: Databricks acquisition itch still unsatisfied -buys Row Zero
item.description:
Databricks has acquired Row Zero and its spreadsheet technology developed for both human and AI agent users.

Row Zero says that it’s a Seattle-based cloud-spreadsheet startup founded in 2021 by former Amazon Web Services engineers Breck Fresen (CEO) and Nick End. They were repeat founders. Their earlier company, Shoefitr, a shoe-fitting startup, was acquired by Amazon in 2015. After that they spent years at AWS: Fresen as a principal engineer on S3, End in product management and later VP of product at Tasso. The starting idea came from their own frustration analyzing large datasets in Excel and Google Sheets, which top out around a million rows and force insecure CSV exports. They built a cloud-native spreadsheet that looks like Excel, runs on AWS, can handle hundreds of millions to a billion rows, connects directly to warehouses such as Snowflake, Redshift, Databricks, Postgres and S3, and supports Python alongside Excel-style formulas. The public product launch came in early 2024.

Patrick Wendell, Co-founder and VP of Engineering at Databricks, said: “As more finance, operations, and go-to-market teams adopt Genie, incorporating a seamless spreadsheet experience is a must-have. We’re super excited to bring the Row Zero team to Databricks, helping us continue to evolve Genie’s capabilities to become the go-to AI coworker for every enterprise team.”

Databricks is folding Row Zero into Genie , its AI coworker, so Genie gains a familiar spreadsheet interface  that business teams can use to explore, model, and collaborate, all on a governed foundation powered by Genie Ontology,  Unity Catalog, and  Unity Gateway.

Spreadsheets were the original data analysis and summation tool, with data warehouses, big data analytics, data lakes and bakehouses being used for the analytics jobs too big for spreadsheets. But spreadsheets were too useful a tool to go away and, as Databricks says, spreadsheets remain the primary engine of business decision-making despite continuous advances in the data and analytics market. Now it’s adding spreadsheet functionality and interface features to its modern Genie AI.

And it’s playing the spreadsheets-are insecure-card to to say Genie+Row Zero is better, saying the prevalence of spreadsheets creates major security and governance challenges for the modern enterprise. Teams have long relied on ungoverned spreadsheet files (“spreadmarts”) to store data or to share between humans and agents. Every data export adds to what is arguably the largest set of ungoverned data pipelines in the enterprise. As companies deploy agents that analyze, model, and act on business data, they can't afford to have those agents operating on sensitive data of unknown lineage and quality.

So, Databricks implies, b uy into the Genie+Row Zero combo because Row Zero offers a scalable spreadsheet that connects directly to live, governed data. This means teams can work the way they always have, backed by built-in security and governance. And because they can work directly with the spreadsheet via Row Zero’s agent tools, every agent action remains fully interpretable and auditable by the business teams using the spreadsheet's syntax and processing model. Row Zero will natively integrate with the Databricks Data + AI Platform , including Genie on web as well as desktop and mobile apps, so teams can easily move from chat to hands-on pivoting, modeling, and visualization.

Acquisition terms were not disclosed, although we understand Row Zero has raised about $13 million at a roughly $40 million valuation.

Co-founder Nick End made an informative LinkedIn post about the acquisition. Breck Fresen, Founder and CEO of Row Zero, said: “We built Row Zero because we love spreadsheets but recognized they needed to seamlessly connect to enterprise-scale data with governance and security at the core. Joining Databricks accelerates our vision of giving business users the spreadsheet they deserve: secure, connected, scalable, and deeply integrated with AI agents.”

The Row Zero team are joining Databricks. Row Zero will be available to all Databricks customers across all major clouds and will continue  to feature support for data sources beyond Databricks.

Bootnote

So far this year Databricks has bought:

  • Quotient AI (March 2026) — tools for evaluating and doing reinforcement learning with AI agents.

  • Antimatter (March 2026) — security startup focused on data protection, authorization, and governance for AI agents, supporting its Lakewatch security lakehouse.

  • SiftD.ai (March 2026) — early-stage security company working on agentic AI–human collaboration and large-scale detection engineering.

  • Panther Labs (agreed June 16, 2026) — AI security operations center (SOC) platform. Databricks described this as its third security acquisition and a step toward an “agentic” security lakehouse that can compete with legacy SIEM tools. Terms were not disclosed; Panther had previously been valued at about $1.4 billion.

  • Electric (August 2026) — maker of PGlite, a lightweight WebAssembly-based Postgres database, plus a real-time sync engine. The goal is to give AI agents a local Postgres instance that can still sync with Databricks’ Lakebase.

CEO Ali Ghodsi has said the company intends to keep making similar acquisitions. Financial terms for most of the 2026 deals have not been disclosed.

item.title: Raspberry Pi surfs memory crunch to record first half
item.description:
Raspberry Pi has posted a record first half after a well-timed memory stockpile helped it ride out soaring prices and shortages.

The Cambridge-based company reported revenue of $256.9 million for the six months ended June 30, up 90 percent from $135.5 million a year earlier, while pre-tax profit more than tripled to $19.6 million.

Raspberry Pi shipped 4.2 million boards during the six-month period, up 17 percent year-on-year, while its order backlog doubled to 2.6 million units.

Behind some of those rather healthy numbers is a bet Raspberry Pi made last year, when it built up a sizeable stash of memory before the market tightened.

"The decision in FY 2025 to build significant strategic memory inventory has allowed us to maintain product availability at a time when smaller competitors have struggled to secure allocation," CEO Eben Upton said. It also meant Raspberry Pi spent much of the first half burning through memory bought at considerably friendlier prices.

Gross profit per board climbed from $8 a year ago to $12.20, helped by price rises on R Pi's products as well as cheaper memory inventory acquired during 2025. Overall gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million.

That particular party is winding down. Raspberry Pi said the "exceptional unit economics" seen in the first half have since moderated as the cheaper memory bought during 2025 has been used up.

It hasn't stopped stockpiling – it's just paying a lot more to do it. The average cost of memory in its inventory stood at $13.30 per GB at the end of June, up from $3.60 per GB at the end of 2025.

At the end of June, Raspberry Pi was holding 2.4 million LPDDR4 devices representing 5.8 million GB of memory. By the end of August, that had grown to 8.3 million GB – around three months of sales for the products that use it.

Between that stockpile and confirmed orders, Raspberry Pi said it has enough memory to meet its production targets for the rest of 2026, with further purchases planned to ensure it enters 2027 with significant inventory.

However, the shortage hasn't left it entirely unscathed. Pi Zero sales fell 9 percent after production congestion at a Taiwanese company packaging one of its core components restricted supply. Demand hasn't disappeared: Raspberry Pi has about 1 million Pi Zero units sitting on back order.

Elsewhere, customers appear willing to swallow the higher prices forced by rising memory costs. Direct sales of Raspberry Pi 4 and Pi 5 boards increased 69 percent and 47 percent respectively, with the company reporting continued demand for the pricier 8GB variants.

OEM customers are also becoming an increasingly important part of the business. Direct shipments rose 26 percent to 3.4 million units, with Raspberry Pi pointing to particularly strong demand from the smart home and aerospace and defense sectors.

The company expects to ship more units in the second half than the first, despite the ongoing squeeze on memory supplies.

For Raspberry Pi, planning for the great memory squeeze has so far been rather more lucrative than painful. Buying the RAM before everyone desperately needed it turned out to be a useful trick. ®

item.title: Windows update leaves some virtual desktops staring into the void
item.description:
Microsoft has admitted that some Windows 11 virtual desktops may fail to load after sign-in, leaving users staring at a black screen until they launch Explorer manually.

The glitch affects devices running the August 2026 non-security preview update or later releases and, according to Microsoft, "has been primarily observed on Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) hosts, using FSLogix."

Windows Explorer crashes may appear in the affected device's Application event log. Users can temporarily recover the desktop by opening Task Manager and running explorer.exe as a new task.

Microsoft has also issued a Known Issue Rollback (KIR) that administrators can deploy through Group Policy. This disables the offending change until a permanent fix arrives. "We are working on a resolution for this issue, and it will be released in a future Windows update," the company said.

This is distinct from another problem introduced by the same August preview update, which replaced some customized desktop backgrounds with solid black . Microsoft fixed that in September, but has not explained precisely what causes this latest failure. It said only that the problem "appears to occur more frequently with some existing user profiles."

That will be of limited comfort to users glumly firing up Task Manager to launch their desktops manually.

Windows 11 versions 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2 are affected. Microsoft does not list Windows 10 or Windows Server among the affected platforms.

The stream of problems introduced by Microsoft's August and September updates is becoming relentless, undermining the company's claims that Windows is getting better. Quality improvement promises made earlier this year by Windows chief Pavan Davuluri are ringing increasingly hollow. If this is how Microsoft plans to "win back" its fans, as Satya Nadella said it must , the response may well be: thanks, but no thanks. ®

item.title: IonQ: There Is One CPU To Rule Error Correction Decoding
item.description:
For all the work being done to get to fault-tolerant, scalable quantum computing – system architectures , the development of software and algorithms, mapping out workflows for classical-quantum hybrid environments – a key bottleneck continues to be error detection and correction . Without it, quantum systems will remain too unreliable – will create too many errors – for practical use.

Strides are being made in this area, with logical qubits playing a central role, comprising myriad noisy physical qubits and acting as the reliable building blocks for quantum systems. That said, another significant part of error correction is decoding, the process of analyzing error signals – or syndromes – generated during error correction to determine the specific errors affecting the system.

Quantum computers can’t directly measure qubits without destroying them. Qubits are extremely fragile and can be easily broken by surround noise – light, vibration, and other qubits, for example, and lose their quantum nature and the data they hold. Instead, they measure surround data points to produce syndromes that indicate an error has occurred and turn the information over to decoders.

“A key challenge in decoding is managing the computational complexity involved, particularly as the size of the quantum system grows,” according to scientists with QuEra , a quantum computing company that uses neutral atoms to build its qubits . “Efficient decoders must balance speed and accuracy, ensuring real-time performance without sacrificing the ability to correctly interpret complex error patterns.”

Decoding is a process that relies heavily on classical computing algorithms and historically has consumed a lot of processing power, which increases as the quantum systems – and the number of qubits – grow. It also has to be tailored to the specific error correction code – like surface code or color codes – that is being used.

Advancements are being made. GPU acceleration, such as through Nvidia’s CUDA-Q platform , is coming into play, as is the use of AI. Recent examples include IBM using a large language model (LLM) framework to sort through thousands of code variations to determine the right one for a particular environment. Google two years ago created AlphaQubit , which uses a transformer-based neural network for decoding and fixing errors, and this year detailed an AI-based reinforcement learning technique that runs the encoded information collected by a quantum computer through an AI system that can learn from the errors found and make adjustments in the system. It would mean operators could run the superconducting quantum computers for long periods of times without having to stop to adjust calibrations when errors are found.

This week, scientists with IonQ, which is building its quantum systems based on the trapped-ion modality, said they’ve developed a decoder that can handle the complex job in real time using a single standard CPU, and can do it in the background, allowing the quantum computer – similar to Google’s reinforcement learning method – to continue running.

“The realization of a MegaQuOp quantum computer, that is a device capable of executing millions of operations on hundreds of logical qubits, represents a major milestone for the quantum computing community and would provide a new tool for scientific exploration,” the scientists wrote in a research paper on arXiv . “However, real-time decoding of hundreds of logical qubits throughout a quantum computation comprising millions of logical operations remains a major challenge.”

IonQ executives said the research shows that organizations don’t need to exponentially scale their classical hardware even as the quantum computers grow their numbers of logical qubits. They added that being able to run error decoding on a classical computer powered by a single CPU is a central to its roadmap (below) that extends well beyond the 256 physical qubits on its Superion system , which it introduced earlier this month.

The vendor announced this week that Florida International University is buying a Superion system (below). It will be installed in late 2027 at a specialized facility on the school’s campus.

In the paper, the scientists wrote that they created benchmark circuits that simulated up to 408 logical qubits across 88 memory blocks and magic factories, or subsystems in fault-tolerant systems that produce the environment needed for universal quantum computing. The circuits ran more than 31.5 million individual quantum operations at the MegaQuOp scale while introducing as little as 0.02 percent stretch time.

Essentially, there was very little delay added to the overall quantum computation, according to the scientists.

They noted other research efforts to accelerate the speed and throughput of surface code – an error-correcting code that protects the quantum information by encoding a single logical qubit across a two-dimensional square grid of physical qubits – and quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) memory decoders through software and hardware, including GPUs, ASICs, FPGAs, and TPUs, to reach the latency needed for superconducting quantum systems.

The IonQ scientists wrote that their decoding system spanned 68 LDPC memory blocks and 20 magic state factories that were created using 11,680 physical qubits. It’s based on a dual sliding-window decoder built around the beam search decoder, an error-correction algorithm for decoding LDPC by ensuring a fixed number of the most promising error pathways – the beam width – at each step. The process creates detector error models (DEMs) in real time and includes memory optimizations that let many decoder instances to execute at the same time on a single CPU.

DEMs are mathematical descriptions that map how gate errors or noise cause particular error detectors in an error-correction circuit.

A key to the CPU-only process is IonQ’s Walking Cat architecture for trapped-ion quantum systems, which the vendor introduced in a detailed blueprint in April. The architecture includes a compiler, error-correction protocols, a microarchitecture, complete simulations, and a fast decoder, all based on an the LDPC error-correction codes. Foundational to the architecture is a “cat factory” that creates cat states – superpositions of distinct states at the same time – that are distributed throughout a system to perform logical operations.

The scientists noted the simplicity of the architecture, writing that “logical computation does not require merging or deforming qLDPC memory blocks or changing their syndrome-extraction circuits.”

Instead, they wrote, “cat-based measurements are inserted into an otherwise regular stream of syndrome extraction, while a large class of Clifford operations (quantum gates that map Pauli operators – X, Y, Z – to other Pauli operators under conjugation) is handled through software frame tracking, making the entire classical decoding pipeline, from online DEM generation to decoding, feasible at MegaQuOp scale using only 12 cores of a single commodity CPU.”

item.title: Uncle Sam wants in on Musk's €120M fight with Brussels
item.description:
The US government wants to join Elon Musk and X's legal challenge to the European Commission's €120 million fine against the social media platform.

The Commission issued its first fine under the Digital Services Act (DSA) in December 2025, finding that X had breached transparency rules through its paid blue checkmarks, advertising repository, and restrictions on researchers' access to public data.

X owner Elon Musk described the decision as "crazy" and "insane" in a Xeet, and compared the "woke" Commission to "Stasi commissars," combining two rather different authoritarian references.

Before issuing a response, he shared the comments made by FCC chair Brendan Carr, who accused "Europe" of "fining a successful US tech company for being a successful US tech company."

"Europe is taxing Americans to subsidize a continent held back by Europe's own suffocating regulations," Carr added.

US politicians also rallied around Musk. Senator Ted Cruz called the fine "an abomination" and an attack on American free speech.

The US government has now applied to intervene in the cases brought by Musk and X Internet and X Holdings, supporting their attempts to annul the Commission's decision.

Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate accused the Commission of regulatory overreach against US companies beyond its jurisdiction.

"The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction," he said .

"We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth."

The Justice Department said it has "significant concerns" about how the Commission determined which people and companies constituted the provider of X's digital service. It intends to argue that the decision conflicts with accepted limits on extraterritorial jurisdiction and the principle that companies are ordinarily legally distinct from their owners and shareholders.

It was especially concerned that the Commission's approach "extended legal scrutiny to Mr Musk himself as a private individual" and implicated other US companies under his control.

According to the DoJ, the Commission found the parties jointly and severally liable for the €120 million fine and calculated it using the worldwide turnover of the corporate group ultimately controlled by Musk. The US government argues that allowing this approach to stand could have broader consequences for American-owned digital platforms operating in the EU.

The DoJ stated: "If the approach in the European Commission Decision is upheld, this may have significant implications for 'very large online platforms' and other similar entities operating in the digital services sector within the EU, many of which are domiciled (at parent level) within the United States.

"The United States looks forward to the opportunity to address these concerns and issues in detail before the General Court."

Musk bought Twitter in 2022 and subsequently replaced its identity-based verification system with a subscription offering. Blue checkmarks, previously awarded by Twitter to accounts it considered authentic and notable, became available to paying users without equivalent identity checks. The change swiftly produced impersonation and spam , and the Commission concluded that presenting those accounts as "verified" amounted to deceptive design.

The Commission also found that X's advertising repository lacked required information and imposed access barriers that prevented effective scrutiny of advertisements. Separately, it said X placed unnecessary obstacles in the way of researchers seeking public platform data.

The violations behind the EU fine are separate from matters under investigation in the UK, including X's handling of illegal hate speech and terrorist content flowing through its feeds and Grok's highly controversial nudifying functionality .

The Commission has since accepted X's plan to address the advertising repository and researcher access violations. The €120 million penalty and the legal theory used to calculate and impose it remain the subjects of the challenges now before the General Court – and, if its application succeeds, of an intervention by the US government. ®

item.title: Asahi fork embraces LLMs and lands Linux on the M4 Mac mini
item.description:
Gravity Linux is a newly announced distro targeting newer Apple Silicon Macs, and its first experimental alpha already boots an accelerated desktop on the M4 Mac mini.

The project homepage says: "Gravity Linux is a Fedora remix that brings a fast, modern Linux desktop to Apple Silicon – built in the open, by people like you."

If this sounds familiar, the About page explains: "Gravity Linux was initially forked from Asahi Linux over differences in policy, namely regarding LLM use. We have tremendous respect for the Asahi Linux project and emphasize our shared goal of running Linux on Apple Silicon."

There's already an early alpha release for the M4 Mac mini, a model launched in October 2024 just days after the company announced the M4 iMac . It includes GPU acceleration with OpenGL ES 3.0 and OpenGL 3.3 support, but is explicitly aimed at developers rather than daily use. HDMI output works, but USB-C displays, USB4, Thunderbolt, and suspend do not, while power management remains incomplete.

In terms of hardware generations, this puts Gravity ahead of Asahi Linux. As The Register reported earlier this month , Asahi has only recently added preliminary M3 support, for now without graphics acceleration. The comparison is not exact, however: Gravity's M4 release is an early developer alpha, while Asahi is a longer-established project supporting a much broader range of hardware. Apple, meanwhile, has already moved on: The Reg reported on the first M6-based Macs last month, nearly three years after the company launched its "scary fast" M3 systems .

The Reg reported on the new Asahi Linux project in March 2022, and tried it out later the same month. However, Asahi has since lost several prominent contributors. Project lead Hector Martin resigned in February 2025 . A week later, the leader of the GPU effort, known only as "Asahi Lina," also quit . As we mentioned later that year , in August 2025, the leader of the GPU driver effort, Alyssa Rosenzweig , left the project. She had already, in her own words, passed the reins on to her other Arm GPU drivers that April. As her resume [PDF] shows, she's been working for Intel since then.

Gravity attributes much of its rapid progress to a development method that Asahi explicitly prohibits. Project lead Cody Ho previously worked at both Apple and OpenAI, and has published a two-part account of using coding agents for Apple Silicon reverse engineering.

On August 3, Ho published the first part of "I Came, I Prompted, I Left," describing the construction of a custom hypervisor for newer Apple Silicon . The second part, published on September 15, explains how he and co-developer Niklas Sheth built an M4 GPU driver in about a month . Ho says much of the work was performed through largely unattended LLM loops.

This is one of the sharpest differences between Gravity Linux and Asahi Linux. Ho and Sheth are reverse-engineering Apple's hardware with the assistance of AI tools, while the Asahi project has a Generative AI (LLM) Policy that says "we broadly forbid the use of generative AI tooling for material contributions to Asahi Linux."

Gravity's LLM Use and Clean-Room Policy permits such tools but attempts to contain the legal risks through separation. It states: "If in any session your LLM has looked at any disassembly, decompilation, or other protected implementation details of an Apple component, you must consider yourself tainted with respect to that component."

This does not mean nobody involved looks at Apple binaries. Ho says that while developing the hypervisor, he used an LLM to disassemble Apple's proprietary SPTM component. That made him ineligible to write the corresponding clean-room implementation, so the knowledge had to be documented and handed to someone who had not seen the protected material.

Ho and Sheth say the GPU work followed a stricter route, using hardware traces, live probing and self-written shaders without inspecting Apple binaries. They also acknowledge benefiting from Asahi's earlier M1 and M2 work and using its existing userspace API.

The result is nevertheless striking: Gravity's first alpha brings an accelerated Linux desktop to an M4 Mac mini, and Ho credits LLMs with helping the pair achieve in weeks work that would ordinarily take far longer. But the code still requires extensive testing, human review, and refactoring before it can be upstreamed. Gravity's developers warn that its kernel driver may have to wait for Asahi's M1 and M2 driver to land upstream first.

Gravity has therefore produced an intriguing demonstration of what AI-assisted reverse engineering can do, rather than a controlled experiment proving that Asahi's policy is what held it back. ®

item.title: Amazon sellers watch as inventory vanishes into pending-order purgatory
item.description:
Traders on Amazon's UK marketplace say a wave of "abnormal" orders stuck in pending status is tying up their inventory and preventing legitimate customers from buying the affected items.

Vendors on Amazon's Seller Central forums report unusually high numbers of pending orders in their accounts, often involving products priced at £100 ($132) or more.

Reports began appearing on September 20. Within days, some sellers – often individuals or small businesses – said their entire stock of certain high-value products had become trapped in pending orders that were not clearing.

Amazon marks an order as pending while it processes and verifies the purchase. The quantity ordered is meanwhile deducted from the seller's available inventory, and sellers cannot cancel the transaction themselves.

Amazon says orders commonly remain pending when it cannot authorize the buyer's credit card or, for business purchases, while they await the customer's approval.

Some merchants suspect deliberate inventory locking: bogus orders reserve stock without completing payment, preventing genuine customers from buying it. They have compared the apparent tactic to a denial-of-service (DoS) attack, although there is no evidence yet that the activity is malicious rather than an Amazon glitch.

Sellers describe activity far outside their usual patterns, in some cases double or triple their typical weekly order volume.

One seller said a product received 30 pending orders in about 52 hours. Among them were 15 orders associated with just seven delivery postcodes.

Another seller reported 72 pending orders worth about £25,000 in three days and wondered whether competitors were using cards without sufficient funds to interfere with its inventory.

Others said Seller Support treated the activity as normal and claimed no other merchants had reported it. That answer frustrated vendors who had found multiple forum threads describing the same problem.

We raised the issue with Amazon after a reader alerted us to the complaints.

A forum message posted several hours after we contacted Amazon said the issue had been escalated to the company's "partner teams" for investigation. The timing may, of course, have been coincidental.

We asked Amazon what was causing the pending orders and whether it regarded the activity as malicious. The company had not responded with an official statement by the time of publication. ®

item.title: BOFH: The Helldesk opens its third eye and ascends to a higher plane of troubleshooting
item.description:
The Boss has had some feedback from the using classes about our method of fixing IT problems (i.e. fixing them), and how we could do things a little better.

"Oh, it will most certainly solve the problem. What I'm proposing is to take about 1 kilobyte of the virus code and then mix it into 1 megabyte of random bytes – THEN I'm going to take 1 kilobyte of that mixed code and mix THAT into another megabyte of random bytes, THEN I'm going to mail it to your computer, which will cause a minor triggering of antivirus, which will make the entire antivirus system stronger."

"Why?"

"Not by itself – but I'm also going to place your laptop in a pyramid that I will shortly construct out of rods of amethyst, which have a calming effect on the aura around your machine – which I will have open and facing due west."

"Uh, why?"

"So it's aligned with the cosmic ley lines. By aligning your laptop with them, the virus and its aura should flow through the ether – not the Ethernet, mind – into the seventh realm of Uranus."

"It sounds like someone's anus is involved," the PFY mumbles unkindly.

"I'm sorry, my assistant has a bit of negative energy, but he will shortly leave the room. Now, how are you feeling about this – positive?"

"I… well, I guess I'm a bit, uh... I'm not sure really."

"Ah, so I'm sensing some doubt – and it doesn't surprise me either, because the feng shui of this room is VERY out of kilter."

"How do you mean?"

"In the first instance, your work center is significantly misaligned because the focal point of personal enterprise should actually be where your doorway is, not where it currently is, and your rubbish bin should actually be in the location that your desk is in. Which probably accounts for your poor work performance."

"Oh – perhaps that was just something your manager was saying. Don't worry about it. Anyway, I think the piles of old paper on your desk are negatively affecting your future vision from your third eye – as they're tying you to the past."

"Well, I think after we move the desk and the bin, we should put that paper in the bin, then move your bookshelf from the west wall to the middle of the room, opening up the aura path to your west-facing laptop."

"Is he OK?" the Boss gasps.

"More or less. The PFY gave him some color therapy by changing his desktop background color to purple. Then he kicked off the antivirus software – which is what we'd have done in the first place... How does that make you feel?"

item.title: Dyfed-Powys Police cops to cyberattack, staff data potentially nicked
item.description:
Dyfed-Powys Police has revealed it was hit by a cyberattack that knocked some of its systems offline, with investigators now trying to establish whether the intruders got their hands on staff data during the break-in.

The Welsh police force said it identified the incident on September 14 and that it caused disruption to some non-emergency systems.

Emergency policing remained operational throughout, according to the force, while its 999 and 101 telephone services were unaffected. Online and email contact were unavailable for a period but have since been restored.

What happened behind the scenes remains less clear. Dyfed-Powys Police said an investigation has been underway since the incident was discovered, with cybersecurity specialists brought in and "precautionary measures" applied to its systems while teams worked to restore services safely.

There’s no indication yet of who was behind the attack, how they got in, or whether ransomware was involved. There is also an unresolved question over what the intruders may have managed to access.

"At this stage, our investigation has found no evidence that members of the public's personal data has been accessed or compromised as a result of this incident," the force said in a statement.

"We are, however, continuing to investigate whether any information relating to our staff may have been accessed or compromised, and are taking all appropriate steps to protect that information, and will provide appropriate advice to colleagues if required."

Dyfed-Powys Police said it has notified the Information Commissioner's Office, although it did not say when the UK data watchdog was informed.

The investigation is being managed by Tarian, the regional organized crime unit covering the three southern Welsh police force areas, through its regional cybercrime unit.

The Register asked Dyfed-Powys Police for more detail about the attack but did not immediately receive a response.

"We understand the potential concern this may cause and want to reassure the public that we have and will continue to take all necessary steps to protect our information and maintain the security of our systems," Dyfed-Powys Police said.

The force says the public's data appears to have escaped the intruders. Whether the same can be said for its staff remains under investigation. ®

item.title: Another week, another data breach for Revolut customers
item.description:
Revolut customers have been caught up in a second data breach this month after attackers socially engineered their way into US brokerage DriveWealth and stole historic personal information.

DriveWealth provides execution and clearing services for investment firms and previously held brokerage accounts directly for Revolut customers trading US stocks. It said the unauthorized access occurred on September 4 and 5.

In an email sent to affected customers and seen by The Register , the broker blamed a "sophisticated social engineering campaign" carried out by unknown third parties.

The intruders exfiltrated data retained from the period when those customers held accounts directly with DriveWealth. The broker said regulatory requirements obliged it to keep the records.

The potentially exposed haul includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, employment information, country of citizenship, age, gender, and partial DriveWealth account numbers.

DriveWealth said it had no reason to believe any other personal information was affected. Passwords and payment information, including credit card and bank account details, were not compromised.

Even so, the exposed details would provide ample material for a convincing phishing message. DriveWealth warned customers that the stolen information could potentially be used for identity fraud, impersonation, further social engineering, or unsolicited contact from strangers.

Revolut customers are among those affected, with the records dating from its previous arrangement with DriveWealth, the company confirmed to the Irish Examiner .

Revolut said its systems and infrastructure were not compromised, and that customer funds and investments remained safe. No Revolut passwords, passcodes, card details, or identity documents were exposed.

The data is a hangover from Revolut's former arrangement for customers trading US stocks. The fintech moved customers in the UK, EEA, and Australia away from that arrangement between December 2023 and June 2025, with the timing varying by market. Their personal details were no longer shared with DriveWealth after the respective migrations.

DriveWealth contacted affected customers directly, while Revolut sent its own notifications. Neither company has disclosed how many Revolut customers were affected, and both failed to answer The Register's questions.

The breach comes at an awkward time for Revolut. On September 14, the fintech admitted it had handed sensitive customer information to criminals after they submitted fraudulent information requests using an email domain belonging to a legitimate government agency.

That separate incident potentially exposed more sensitive information, including passports, driver's licenses, verification selfies, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and financial and transaction data.

Revolut said at the time that it had fallen victim to a "sophisticated external impersonation scam" and that only a limited number of customers were affected.

Two different incidents, two different sets of attackers, and two different routes to customer data. For Revolut customers, September has provided more breach notifications than anyone would want from their banking app. ®

item.title: Judge uses electronic tag on Pokémon card tracker. It's super effective!
item.description:
A 72-year-old Ohio man who planted a GPS tracker on a Pokémon card delivery van has been sentenced to a year of probation – including 90 days wearing a tracker of his own.

Kent Kubasta, of Medina, Ohio, attached a Spytec device to the woman's van. She discovered it while making a delivery to Walmart on June 18 and was described in court documents as "a carrier/vendor of Pokémon cards."

Kubasta initially pleaded not guilty to illegal use of a tracking device, but later waived his right to trial and pleaded no contest. Court records say he placed the device on the van to follow local card deliveries.

For his crime, Kubasta was sentenced [PDF] to 12 months of community control – Ohio's term for probation – under basic supervision. He will be electronically monitored by GPS for the first 90 days.

He was also ordered to have no contact with the woman, pay a $25 monthly supervision fee and a $500 fine, and cover court costs. His total bill comes to $905.50. Violating the terms could land Kubasta in jail for six months.

The court documents do not explain what Kubasta intended to do with the delivery information. The case nevertheless comes amid intense demand for Pokémon cards, with collectors regularly queuing outside shops when new stock arrives.

Pokémon began in 1996 with a pair of Nintendo Game Boy games about catching and battling monsters, and has since evolved into a multibillion-dollar media franchise spanning video games, trading cards, animated television and films, mobile apps, toys, and more.

The latest Trading Card Game expansion , released on September 16, contains more than 150 cards, including 30 rare Pikachu variants, with one included in every booster pack.

Randy Kendall, manager of Operation Fandom in Wooster, where the complaint was filed, told Fox 8 that Pokémon "is absolutely the hottest thing going" and the trading cards are among the store's best-selling products.

Some especially rare examples sell for six or even seven-figure sums, although most collectors manage to pursue them without putting the delivery driver under surveillance. ®

item.title: SPONSORED:
item.description:
EVENT: The Register is hosting a private dinner in Soho on Tuesday 20 October for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders, with LucidLink. Joe Fay takes the chair, it runs under the Chatham House Rule, and nothing said is on the record.

The problem on the table is the one most organisations have stopped saying out loud. Unstructured file data keeps growing, distributed teams keep needing to reach it, and the infrastructure underneath is still legacy NAS, a VPN and a sync-and-download habit nobody actually chose. It rarely fails outright. It just charges rent somewhere else: in duplicated storage, in waiting, in governance gaps, and in the hour somebody loses working out which copy of a file is the current one.

The conversation worth having about that is not the architecture diagram. It is what a team did when it stopped being in one building. Which workaround somebody has quietly been paying for ever since. What broke when they tried to retire the NAS, and what they would do differently. People say that over dinner. They do not say it on a recorded webinar.

So this is dinner. Drinks, a handful of questions across the table, then more drinks. Everyone there as a peer, and a chair whose job includes stopping anyone who starts to pitch.

The premise is deliberately not rip and replace. The evening is about modernising around the storage and governance investments an organisation already has, rather than pretending they are not there, which is usually the point at which these conversations stop being useful to anyone who has to pay for them.

On the table: how organisations are handling the growth in unstructured data, how they support distributed teams without paying for the same file three times, what they do about sync and version control, and whether any of it holds up against a security incident.

Rupert Watson, VP GTM for EMEA at LucidLink, joins the conversation. Joe Fay of The Register moderates.

The table is for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders carrying this now, not planning for it later. Dinner runs from 6.30pm to 9.00pm at The Soho Hotel, 4 Richmond Mews. Places are limited and go by invitation.

item.title: UK wants more homes heated by waste heat from datacenters
item.description:
The UK government says it is pumping £90 million ($119 million) into building and improving heat networks that redirect excess heat energy generated by a datacenter or factory and use it to warm homes or for other purposes.

According to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), more than 750,000 homes will get cheaper heating as part of the scheme, which includes plans for a “mega heat project” that involves distributing hot water via a tunnel under the River Thames.

The latter initiative is being backed by £41 million ($54 million) in funding and the department claims it will supply 650,000 London homes alone with "clean heat." This is designed to make the capital less reliant on gas - similar schemes have operated for decades in cities like Copenhagen, Amsterdam, Vienna and Berlin.

The Register reported on a project back in 2023 that planned to connect 10,000 new homes in west London with nearby server farms to use their waste energy for heating.

Given the glacial pace of progress on any UK project these days, the first question must be when this is likely to happen. The recently completed Thames “ super sewer ” project took 9 years to finish and cost about £5 billion ($6.6bn), leading The Reg to wonder whether tunnels for the heat project will ever actually be dug, and what the final price tag will be.

In the absence of pipes in tunnels, the government says the hot water will initially be transported 25 kilometers (15 miles) along the Thames each day by electric barges from a waste plant near Bexley, a faintly ridiculous idea that has prompted inevitable outbursts of scorn from the usual highbrow commenters on social media.

A spokesperson for DESNZ told us the £41 million funding is just for the barge part of the project, which is expected to start operating from 2028, while it hopes the tunnels will be operational in the 2030s. There is currently no information on how much that potion of the project will cost.

There is also the question of whether using the waste heat from datacenters is really that efficient. It was previously noted by the Uptime Institute that the temperature is typically not high enough for applications including domestic heating, so a heat pump is required, which uses more energy.

A 2024 report released by trade association TechUK claimed that while the latest fifth generation of heat network designs can operate with the lower temperature output from a computer shed, most operating in the UK are third-gen systems, which have lower energy efficiency and higher carbon intensity.

Despite these doubts, a survey finds that about 60 percent of British people think planning permission for datacenters should be dependent on them supplying their excess heat to local homes and businesses, while 62 percent said they would be more supportive of a project in their area if it did commit to this.

The polling was conducted by EnergiRaven, a firm advising on energy efficiency, which calls for all new server farms above 1 MW in capacity to include heat sharing infrastructure.

As bit barn development continues to draw controversy, sharing waste heat could give operators another way to demonstrate their value to local communities, helping to build greater public support for new facilities, the firm claims.

Alan Howard of tech analyst group Omdia commented: "District heating is certainly a win for any community, and for datacenters it may shine a positive light as some communities are hesitant to embrace them. What’s known so far… doesn’t reveal if the focus is on exploiting existing datacenters, which would [be] its own can of worms, or encouraging and supporting new datacenters to support the heating proposal."

Howard added: "Of course, anything that might lighten the dependence on gas dependence is a win as well. It’s too early to call it a project, rather at this stage it is a concept. However, the government commitment is impressive and important to make such sweeping changes and upgrades to what sounds to be an aging and perhaps inefficient existing system."


Omdia's Howard tells The Reg : "Obviously, of the many risk characteristics for such and undertaking there are a few that stand out: As a government led project the actual progress and timeline could be messy and long. The engineering for such a significant effort (“transporting hot water 25 km each day by electric barges “, not to mention the tunnels under the Thames) is certain to find a litany of challenges to overcome- While the funding sounds significant, real world experience in construction of seemingly exotic projects could easily balloon many time over."

Other heat networks that can expect multi-million-pound investment from the DESNZ include an extension to an existing system in Solihull in England’s midlands, a project at Marble Arch in London serving offices, homes, hotels and businesses around Oxford Street, and another in London at Bexley and Greenwich that may serve up to 100,000 homes when fully built. ®
